newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Capos offered to testify against Colombia's Samper.
newsitem.headline: Capos offered to testify against Colombia's Samper.

text.p: The jailed leaders of Colombia's Cali drug mob offered to provide the United States with proof of President Ernesto Samper's alleged ties to the narcotics trade, U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette said on Wednesday.

"Yes, they told it to me," Frechette said in a television interview, when asked if brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela had ever tried to cut a deal with the United States in exchange for more lenient treatment by U.S. judicial officials.
"I answered back, through the same channels, that we weren't interested in reaching any agreement with them," he added. "What we want is that they be tried and be punished for their crimes."

Frechette's remarks, on Colombia's QAP televison news programme, marked his first public comment to date on widely rumoured offers by the Rodriguez brothers -- who were jailed in 1995 -- to turn state evidence against Samper in exchange for some sort of truce with the United States.
A U.S. request for their extradition, in the summer of last year, has gone unanswered by the Colombian government.

U.S. officials cited corruption at the "highest levels" of the Colombian government, and Samper's alleged financing of his 1994 campaign with Cali cartel drug money, as among the reasons Washington "decertified" the Andean nation as a trustworthy ally in the drug war last week.
In the TV interview, Frechette said the U.S. government was not interested in "persecuting President Samper."

The embattled Colombian leader was cleared by Colombia's Congress in June 1996 of any wrongdoing in connection with his campaign. But the U.S. State Department described Samper's congressional trial as "flawed" in a statement last week explaining the reasons behind the decision to decertify Colombia for a second year.

In the interview, Frechette reiterated earlier U.S. allegations that the Rodriguezes, heads of an organisation that once controlled up to 80 percent of the world's cocaine market, continued to run their criminal empire from behind the walls of Bogota's La Picota prison.

He also said that a decision by Samper earlier on Wednesday, to suspend the aerial spraying of Colombia's illicit drug crops with herbicide, would spell "disaster" for U.S.-Colombian ties if it was anything more than temporary.
